# Correcting the bias against interdisciplinary research

## Authors

- Ehud Shapiro<sup>1</sup> †

### Affiliations

1. Department of Computer Science and Applied Math and Department of Biological Chemistry Weizmann Institute of Science Rehovot Israel ehud.shapiro@weizmann.ac.il

† Corresponding author

## Abstract

When making decisions about funding and jobs the scientific community should recognise that most of the tools used to evaluate scientific excellence are biased in favour of established disciplines and against interdisciplinary research.

## Is there really a bias against interdisciplinary research?

One objective measure of the bias against interdisciplinary research is provided by the success rates of researchers who apply to the European Research Council (ERC) for ERC Advanced Grants and ERC Starting Grants. Although excellence is the sole selection criterion used to award these grants, the success rate for applications categorised as interdisciplinary has been lower than the success rate for single-discipline applications in each of the first four years of these schemes (Labastida, 2013).

Such objective measures of the bias against interdisciplinary research are very difficult to come by, yet subjective and/or personal experiences are commonplace. It seems a common occurrence for research outside of the well-established disciplines to be rejected outright by journal editors as uninteresting to the community. Furthermore, even if a submitted manuscript passes the initial screen, the editor may have difficulties finding referees who have the expertise needed to review the paper.

And when it comes to nourishing particular disciplines, those in positions of power—such as department heads in universities or programme managers at funding agencies—face the daily grind of a zero-sum struggle for resources. This means that they are often only able or willing to support interdisciplinary research with lab space or research grants if doing so does not erode the resources available to researchers working in that particular discipline. This inevitably tips the scales against researchers who do not fit comfortably into any existing discipline.

## How and why does the bias arise?

Most researchers work in what could be termed ‘dense scientific communities’. By this I mean well-established scientific communities in which the different members attend the same meetings, publish in the same journals, cite each other’s papers and often collaborate and compete with each other. In such dense scientific communities, the goals of the field are well defined and well known, and are addressed simultaneously by many scientists in a competitive way, much like an Olympic race. Moreover, in such communities the preferred venues for the publication of new results—high-impact journals in some communities, competitive conferences in others—are also widely recognised and community members are more than willing to review manuscripts written by their colleagues, because it helps them to stay on top of the competition and to be inspired by yet-unpublished research. Publications in such communities also get cited quite rapidly and in large numbers, by the many peers working in the same area.

In dense scientific communities, the ‘elders’ are well recognised and have the authority to set the rules by which excellence in this community is measured. These elders are also forthcoming with letters of recommendation for their best intellectual offspring. Young researchers who play by the rules and successfully address problems that have been deemed important by the elders are rewarded handsomely and, over time, these young researchers become elders themselves, thus ensuring that the community continues to flourish.

This situation is in stark contrast to that of researchers operating at and between the boundaries of established disciplines. Genuine interdisciplinary research is nothing like a competitive race. It is much more like a solitary exploratory hike through an uncharted landscape. There are no community elders to give guidance, to define and rank the important research goals, or to write recommendation letters to their intellectual offspring. There are no peers to compete with or use as reviewers; and there are no community-specific journals or conferences. In general, the intricate and encompassing community support structure present in dense scientific communities is completely missing. Often the best that one can hope for is to recruit unsuspecting students as company for the journey.

All this means that many of the so-called ‘objective measures’ that are used to assess researchers—such as impact factors (with all their flaws), citation counts, or letters of recommendation—are highly biased in favour of researchers who belong to dense scientific communities at the expense of those who are members of sparse scientific communities.

## Why should we care and what can we do?

Although recognising excellence at and between the boundaries of established disciplines is difficult, it is essential that we keep trying to identify scientists who have the potential to make real breakthroughs in these areas. If these scientists are not identified and funded, then—almost by definition—certain highly promising interdisciplinary areas might remained unexplored because no one else is working in them. This is not a problem in dense scientific communities: if we fail to recognise and support the very best person working towards a particular important goal in this field, then someone else will probably reach the same goal, albeit with some delay. Unfair as it may be, the progress of science is relatively unaffected by such an outcome. Hence, as rare as excellence may be in the outback of interdisciplinary research, it should be actively sought, identified and rewarded even more than excellence in dense communities.

How can we ensure that excellence in areas other than established disciplines is actively sought, identified and rewarded even more than excellence in dense scientific communities? First we must recognise that the three tools that are most widely used to evaluate researchers—measures based on impact factors, citation counts and recommendation letters—are highly biased in favour of members in dense communities. Once we do, the next step should be to actively correct this bias.

For example, one code-word used for rejecting interdisciplinary grant proposals is ‘over-ambitious’. This often stands for saying that the scientist intends to do something that is radically different from what has been done until now and does not follow the ‘rules’ of the reviewer’s home scientific community. Perhaps such judgments should be banned. What is wrong with being over-ambitious? Besides, the predictability of a scientific endeavour is arguably inversely proportional to how innovative it is. So maybe any scientific project that is not ‘over-ambitious’ is by definition not innovative enough?

A useful countermeasure would be to develop an objective measure of the density of various scientific communities that could be taken into account when making decisions about funding and jobs. If two scientists are judged equal on the basis of the standard measures, then the scientist from the less dense community (see figure) could be ranked higher to compensate for the biases against researchers in these areas.

![Figure.](https://cdn.elifesciences.org/articles/02576/elife-02576-fig1-v1.jpg)

**Figure.:** The social network of a particular scientist, say Mary Smith (red circle), consists of all the scientists (blue circles) cited by Mary or citing Mary, with edges connecting those scientists who have cited each other. The resulting network will lie somewhere between two extremes: a maximally dense network (right), in which all the scientists in the network cite each other, and a maximally sparse network (left) in which there are no citations among the scientists except citations by or to Mary.

More sophisticated analysis could also be applied. For example, it would be useful to identify dense scientific communities that receive very little input from, and exert very little influence over, other fields of science; decisions to fund such ‘mutual-admiration societies’ should be subject to higher than usual levels of scrutiny. Conversely, scientists who have integrated two previously unrelated areas of research to open up completely new fields of inquiry could also be identified by such an analysis, and recognised accordingly.

More research should be devoted to measuring the density of scientific communities (probably based on various techniques from graph theory), and more thought should be given as to how this measure can be factored into the evaluation of scientific excellence. Let me be clear, however: any such correction is not intended to compensate an interdisciplinary scientist for his or her personal hardships. Rather, such a correction is needed to prevent seemingly objective evaluation tools from misleading us and, as a result, holding back scientific progress by diverting funds and jobs from people who have the potential to perform truly ground-breaking science.

results.result: Interdisciplinary applications to ERC Advanced Grants and ERC Starting Grants have lower success rates than single-discipline applications despite excellence being the sole selection criterion. This pattern held consistently across the first four years of these grant schemes.
results.evaluation: Claims C2 and C3 rely entirely on a single citation (Labastida, 2013) without presenting the actual data or statistical analysis. The manuscript does not provide effect sizes, confidence intervals, or control for confounding variables (e.g., application quality, reviewer composition, or field-specific differences). Without access to the underlying data or independent verification, the robustness of this empirical claim cannot be assessed.

results.result: Objective measures of bias against interdisciplinary research are rare, but subjective experiences are common. These include journal editors rejecting interdisciplinary work as uninteresting and difficulty finding qualified reviewers for interdisciplinary manuscripts.
results.evaluation: Claims C4-C7 are based entirely on anecdotal observations and general assertions without systematic evidence. No survey data, publication statistics, or controlled studies are provided to substantiate the frequency or prevalence of these experiences. The claims conflate personal observations with generalizable patterns, lacking the empirical foundation needed to support them as established facts.

results.result: Resource allocation in academic institutions operates as a zero-sum game where department heads and program managers can only support interdisciplinary research if it doesn't reduce resources for their own discipline, creating systematic bias against interdisciplinary researchers.
results.evaluation: Claims C8-C10 present a causal model of institutional behavior without empirical support. No data on actual resource allocation decisions, budget analyses, or institutional case studies are provided. The zero-sum framing is asserted rather than demonstrated, and alternative explanations (e.g., risk aversion, evaluation difficulty) are not considered. This remains a plausible hypothesis but lacks supporting evidence.

results.result: Dense scientific communities are characterized by well-defined goals, shared publication venues, rapid citation accumulation, recognized authority structures, and self-perpetuating reward systems. Members attend common meetings, cite each other frequently, and compete in well-defined races toward established objectives.
results.evaluation: Claims C11-C21 provide a coherent descriptive framework of dense scientific communities based on observable sociological patterns in science. While no quantitative data is presented, these characteristics align with established understanding of disciplinary communities in sociology of science. The claims are internally consistent and represent reasonable generalizations about how established scientific fields operate, though they remain qualitative descriptions rather than empirically tested hypotheses.

results.result: Interdisciplinary research lacks the support structures of dense communities, including community elders, peer reviewers, dedicated journals/conferences, and competitive frameworks. It resembles solitary exploration rather than competitive races.
results.evaluation: Claims C22-C27 provide a logical contrast to the dense community framework, describing structural disadvantages faced by interdisciplinary researchers. These observations are consistent with documented challenges in interdisciplinary science and follow logically from the definition of sparse networks. While qualitative, the characterization is internally coherent and aligns with known features of interdisciplinary work.

results.result: Standard evaluation tools (impact factors, citation counts, recommendation letters) are systematically biased in favor of researchers in dense scientific communities and against those in sparse interdisciplinary communities.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C28, and C35 present the manuscript's central thesis but rely primarily on logical inference from the structural differences between dense and sparse communities rather than direct empirical evidence. While the reasoning is plausible—dense communities naturally generate higher citation counts and more recommendation letters—no quantitative analysis demonstrates that these metrics systematically undervalue equivalent quality work in sparse communities. The argument would require controlling for actual research quality/impact to establish bias rather than just differential outcomes.

results.result: Identifying and funding excellent interdisciplinary scientists is more critical than supporting those in dense communities because failure to do so leaves promising areas unexplored, whereas dense communities have redundancy that ensures important goals are eventually reached.
results.evaluation: Claims C29-C34 present a normative argument about research priorities based on assumptions about redundancy and uniqueness. While the logic is internally consistent, it rests on unverified premises: that interdisciplinary areas are indeed 'highly promising' (C31), that dense communities truly have sufficient redundancy (C32), and that scientific progress is 'relatively unaffected' by funding decisions in dense fields (C33). These are empirical questions requiring evidence about innovation patterns, breakthrough origins, and counterfactual outcomes.

results.result: The term 'over-ambitious' is used as a code-word to reject interdisciplinary proposals that don't follow established community rules. Since predictability is inversely related to innovation, projects that aren't 'over-ambitious' may not be innovative enough.
results.evaluation: Claims C36-C39 make assertions about grant review practices and the relationship between ambition and innovation without supporting evidence. No analysis of review comments, rejection patterns, or systematic study of innovation metrics is provided. Claim C38 presents a general principle without citation or justification, and C39 is explicitly speculative (posed as a rhetorical question). These remain interesting hypotheses but lack empirical foundation.

results.result: An objective measure of scientific community density could be developed using citation network analysis, where a scientist's network ranges from maximally sparse (no citations among peers) to maximally dense (all peers cite each other). This measure could be used to adjust evaluation rankings to compensate for structural biases.
results.evaluation: Claims C40-C43 propose a methodological solution with conceptual clarity (the network density framework is well-defined in C42-C43), but no actual implementation, validation, or testing is provided. Critical questions remain unaddressed: How would density thresholds be set? How would this interact with field-specific citation practices? Would this actually correlate with research quality? The proposal is conceptually sound but requires empirical development and validation before it can be considered a supported solution.

results.result: Network analysis could identify insular 'mutual-admiration societies' that warrant increased funding scrutiny, and could also identify bridging scientists who integrate previously unrelated research areas.
results.evaluation: Claims C44-C46 propose applications of network analysis without demonstrating feasibility or validity. No methods are specified for distinguishing legitimate dense communities from 'mutual-admiration societies,' nor for identifying truly innovative bridging work versus superficial connections. The proposals lack operational definitions, validation criteria, or consideration of false positives/negatives. These remain speculative suggestions for future work.

results.result: Future research should develop graph-theory-based measures of community density and integrate them into excellence evaluation. Such corrections aim to prevent evaluation tools from misleading funding decisions and diverting resources from potentially groundbreaking interdisciplinary scientists.
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C51 present clear recommendations for future work and clarify the rationale for proposed corrections (preventing bias rather than compensating hardship). These normative claims follow logically from the manuscript's arguments, even though the underlying empirical premises remain uncertain. As recommendations for future research direction, they are appropriately framed and internally consistent with the manuscript's thesis.
